item.title: Do You Want to Be Cared For—or Desired?
item.description:
Relationships

Do You Want to Be Cared For—or Desired?

Is caring the essence of romantic love?

Posted September 19, 2026

Key points
  • Caring, desire, reciprocity, and shared activities are central features of romantic love.
  • Desire is more distinctive to romantic love; caring is more important for its endurance.
  • Profound romantic love is strongest when caring and desire reinforce one another.

Romantic love involves several characteristics, including caring, shared activities, desire, admiration, and reciprocity. Ideally, a flourishing relationship contains all of them. But if you had to choose between being cared for and being desired, which would matter more? And which is more fundamental to romantic love?

The Care Model of Love

"I love my house too much to leave my husband." —A married woman

Love is often defined in terms of caring for the beloved's needs. Caring goes beyond positive feelings or simply wanting to be together. It involves genuine concern for another person's well-being and flourishing. As Erich Fromm (1956) wrote, love is "the active concern for the life and growth of that which we love." Emmanuel Levinas (1998) similarly emphasized unconditional concern for the other, even without reciprocity. The care model is especially relevant to unequal relationships, such as parental love, love of God, or caring for a seriously ill partner. In such relationships, one-sided devotion may be entirely appropriate.

Romantic love, however, is typically a relationship between equals. Here, caring is crucial, but reciprocity, shared experiences, desire, positive responsiveness, and mutual flourishing also matter. Caring alone may therefore be neither the essence nor a sufficient condition of romantic love. The question, then, is whether romantic love should be understood primarily as caring—or whether desire and other romantic elements are equally central. One way to approach this question is to distinguish between being cared for and being desired.

Being Desired and Being Cared For

"To love is nothing. To be loved is something. But to love and be loved, that's everything." —T. Tolis

A loving couple
Source: pexels-29997777-4699299

Falling in love and staying in love involve two broad forms of positive evaluation: attractiveness and praiseworthiness. Attractiveness functions like a magnet. It draws us toward another person and often sparks the wish to establish or deepen a romantic bond. Praiseworthiness reflects qualities we admire, respect, or value, such as wisdom, kindness, integrity, or achievement. These dimensions overlap, but they are not identical.

Being desired primarily reflects attraction. Being cared for primarily reflects concern for one's well-being. Caring is generally broader and more stable, whereas desire tends to be more sensitive to circumstances and more difficult to sustain at the same intensity. Caring is also characteristic of friendship and parental love. Desire—especially sexual desire—is far more distinctive to romantic relationships.

article continues after advertisement

This distinction reveals an important paradox: desire may be what makes love uniquely romantic, while caring may be what helps it endure. Desire often fuels the initial bond between partners. Yet desire frequently diminishes with familiarity and time. Caring, by contrast, can remain stable and even deepen throughout a relationship. Caring without desire may gradually transform romance into companionship. Desire without caring may generate passion without creating a profound bond. Romantic love lies between these extremes, combining attraction, concern, reciprocity, and a shared life (Ben-Ze’ev, 2019).

What People Say

People discussing on Reddit the difference between being desired and being loved often capture this tension:

"I would prefer to be loved than to be desired. I've had many men put me on pedestals, projected their fantasies onto me, seen me as someone to be desired, and it's not all roses."

"There is something sexy and carnal about pure desire. Being loved and valued is end game, but don't we all want to be desired, especially by our partner?"

"I've been desired, and it's nice, but desire in the absence of love feels empty to me. You need both!"

"Once you've experienced love and lust together, one without the other sounds hellish."

article continues after advertisement

These comments point to a fundamental tension. Being desired can make us feel attractive and alive; being cared for can make us feel valued, secure, and significant. Most people want both, even if their relative importance changes over time.

The Connection Between Desire and Caring

"We sapiosexuals are sexually attracted to highly intelligent people, regardless of looks." —Marlène Schiappa

Although desire and caring are distinct, they can reinforce one another. Research on the attractiveness halo suggests that physically attractive people across cultures are often perceived as more intelligent, sociable, and morally admirable (Batres & Shiramizu, 2023). The reverse process can also occur. Qualities such as intelligence, kindness, humor, and wisdom can enhance a person's attractiveness. In this sense, attraction and positive evaluation can mutually strengthen each other. The phenomenon of sapiosexuality illustrates this dynamic: for some people, intelligence itself becomes a significant source of sexual attraction. The boundaries between being desired and being cared for are therefore more fluid than they may initially appear.

So, Which Matters More?

"If you live to be a hundred, I want to live to be a hundred minus one day so I never have to live without you." —A. A. Milne

If love means concern for another person's flourishing, caring is indispensable. Without genuine caring, desire can become shallow or self-serving. But if we ask what makes love specifically romantic, desire assumes a distinctive role. Caring for a romantic partner is not fundamentally different from caring for a close friend or family member. Romantic desire introduces something distinctive: the longing for intimate connection with this particular person.

This does not mean that desire must remain as intense as it was at the beginning. Profound romantic love can survive fluctuations in sexual passion. Indeed, enduring love often transforms early desire into a broader and deeper form of intimacy. The strongest romantic relationships may therefore not require choosing between being cared for and being desired. Instead, they involve finding ways for the two to coexist and reinforce each other.

Concluding Thoughts

"If you love without lust, you have a best friend. If you lust without love, you have a friend with benefits. If you have both, you have a long-term romantic relationship." —A woman

Caring is present in almost every form of love. What makes romantic love distinctive is the addition of romantic and sexual desire directed toward a particular person. Yet neither caring nor desire is sufficient on its own. Profound romantic love ideally combines both.

article continues after advertisement

The challenge is that they do not always develop at the same pace. Desire often begins intensely and may weaken with familiarity, whereas caring frequently grows deeper over time. The task of enduring romance is therefore not to choose between being cared for and being desired, but to sustain a relationship in which partners remain both deeply cared for and genuinely desired as their love matures.

item.title: Why Your Apologies Are Not Enough for Your Adult Child
item.description:
Forgiveness

Why Your Apologies Are Not Enough for Your Adult Child

3 ways your apologies can make things worse.

Posted September 19, 2026

Key points
  • With relief-driven apologies, the "I'm sorry" reads as "please forgive me so I can stop feeling bad."
  • The moment that dreaded "but" shows up, the apology is over in your adult child's ears and mind.
  • A better apology is shorter, undefended, and asks for nothing back.

Every week I hear the same story from parents of struggling adult children: "I've apologized. Nothing changes." These parents admit (often readily) that they were too strict, too controlling, or perhaps too permissive. They may have missed identifying (or following up on) their adult child’s anxiety when they were younger, or maybe did not follow up on addressing depression, ADHD, or learning problems. Parents who divorced also acknowledge that the divorce left scars. So why do these parents who say they are sorry (often many times) find their apologies only make things worse?

Leah Apologized to No Avail

Let's take a quick look at a mother that we can call Leah. She apologized to her 27-year-old son, Dan, three times in one year for how strict she'd been growing up. To Leah's dismay, each apology (I'm sorry I made you feel that way") made Dan more distant and quieter, not warmer. After the third one, he stopped responding to her texts and calls for a few weeks. What didn't help was that Leah went into what I call "constantly taking the temperature mode," flooding Dan with even more repeated messages, essentially the same, "just checking to see if you are okay."

Leah wasn't wrong to apologize, but she was wrong about what an apology needs to do, and who it's actually for. When Dan finally responded, he told Leah the apologies felt artificial (Mom, "I'm sorry you feel that way does not cut it). Dan elaborated, saying it was like a performance she needed him to watch. In other words, Leah's apologies didn't land well because Dan felt they didn't match what he saw as a legitimate apology.

This is the pattern of problematic apologies I write about in my book You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me! From the parents' perspective, they are doing all the work in the relationship and get none of the change back. A faulty apology is often part of that pattern, repeated for years without anyone noticing it isn't working. My point here is that if you are going to apologize to your adult child, then make it count.

Here's what usually goes wrong when parents go down the "Bad Apology Expressway:"

1. The Apology Secretly Asks for Something Back

When I coach parents of adult children and help them unpack their failed apologies, they learn that most apologies aren't apologies; they're requests. Your adult child hears "please forgive me" as a way to take away your pain, not theirs. I get that parents want relief and even want their adult child to say it's okay, to soften, to move on. But in these types of relief-driven apologies, the"I'm sorry" reads as "please forgive me so I can stop feeling bad," and now the emotional messiness lands right back on the parents.

2. The Apology Explains More Than It Owns

When you tie the apology to explaining (usually it's overexplaining) the circumstances, it convolutes, dilutes, and outright refutes the apology you are trying to give. For example, "I'm sorry I was so strict, but I was scared for you." Or, "I'm sorry about the divorce, but your father and I tried everything we could."

article continues after advertisement

The moment that dreaded "but" shows up, the apology is over in your adult child's ears and mind. They stop hearing remorse, and because it starts screaming as a case for your own defense. Once it feels like your apology is about proving a point, then they check out, and the next apology starts from a deeper hole.

3. It's Timed for Your Guilt, Not Their Readiness

You apologize after the hard phone call, the sleepless night, that enduring memory that won't quit. That's your timeline, but it may not be your adult child's. Dropped on them uninvited, an apology becomes one more thing they now have to manage on your behalf, on top of whatever they were already carrying that day. A better apology is shorter, undefended, and asks for nothing back. For example, you could say, "I've thought about how strict I was when you were growing up. I was wrong, and I understand if it still affects you." Then stop talking (the hardest part for all of us as parents). So please do yourself a huge favor: don't fill the silence, and don't ask what they're thinking.

Final Thoughts

You can't out-explain or over-apologize your way out of the past. You can only demonstrate, consistently and without announcing it, that you've changed, and let your adult child decide, on their own timeline, when to believe it.
